props.title: Close-Up
props.initialSlug: Reality and Fiction. Two sides of the same truth.

sections.content: Close-Up revolutionized documentary-fiction hybrid filmmaking through Abbas Kiarostami's ingenious recreation of a real-life case where cinephile Hossein Sabzian impersonated director Mohsen Makhmalbaf. The film's meta-commentary on cinema's power to shape identity predates similar experiments like Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010) and The Act of Killing (2012). Kiarostami's masterstroke was casting the actual people to replay their own roles, creating an uncanny blend of truth and performance that questions the very nature of authenticity.

sections.content: Kiarostami's influence on self-reflexive cinema rippled through world film. Synecdoche, New York (2008) took the meta-theatrical concept to surreal extremes, while Stories We Tell (2012) used recreation to explore family truth. The Iranian New Wave that Close-Up epitomized gave rise to similarly boundary-pushing works like Jafar Panahi's This Is Not a Film (2011), shot while under house arrest.

The film's innovative courtroom scenes, where actual trial footage meshes with recreations, influenced later hybrid documentaries like The Thin Blue Line (1988) and Little Dieter Needs to Fly (1997). Kiarostami's compassionate approach to Sabzian's deception reveals cinema's unique ability to excavate human truth through artifice. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Iranian New Wave Cinema

sections.content: Close-Up marked a turning point for Iranian cinema's global recognition, paving the way for masterworks like A Separation (2011) and The Salesman (2016). Kiarostami's signature long takes and car conversations became stylistic touchstones, influencing filmmakers from Jia Zhangke to Richard Linklater. The film's examination of class divisions through the lens of cultural aspiration remains startlingly relevant.
